questions.q: Which two mechanisms allow the kidney to produce concentrated urine?
questions.explain: The loop of Henle builds the gradient. The vasa recta preserve it.

open.q: Which two mechanisms allow the kidney to produce concentrated urine?

questions.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent multiplier?
questions.explain: The loop multiplies a small horizontal gradient into a large vertical one.

open.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent multiplier?

questions.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent exchanger?
questions.explain: Blood flows in a hairpin, taking up water from the medulla without washing out its solutes.

open.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent exchanger?

questions.q: What is the maximum osmolality the human kidney can reach in urine?
questions.explain: It is limited by the medullary gradient. Plasma is about 300 mOsm/L.

open.q: What is the maximum osmolality the human kidney can reach in urine?

questions.q: What is the main transport feature of the thick ascending limb?
options: It is water-impermeable and reabsorbs Na+, K+ and 2Cl−
It is highly permeable to water
It reabsorbs water under ADH control
questions.explain: NKCC2 pumps solutes out while water stays in, so the fluid becomes dilute. This is the diluting segment.

open.q: What is the main transport feature of the thick ascending limb?

questions.q: Is the tubular fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic compared with plasma?
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb removes solute without water, leaving the fluid at about 100 mOsm/L.

open.q: Is the tubular fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic compared with plasma?

questions.q: Which solutes mainly create the high osmolality of the renal medulla?
questions.explain: NaCl is pumped out of the ascending limb. Urea is recycled from the collecting duct.

open.q: Which solutes mainly create the high osmolality of the renal medulla?

questions.q: Which hormone makes the collecting duct permeable to water so that urine can be concentrated?
questions.explain: Without ADH, the collecting duct stays water-impermeable and dilute urine is passed.

open.q: Which hormone makes the collecting duct permeable to water so that urine can be concentrated?

questions.q: What causes central diabetes insipidus?
options: Lack of kidney response to ADH
questions.explain: Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary reduces ADH. It responds to desmopressin.

open.q: What causes central diabetes insipidus?

questions.q: What causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
options: Failure of ADH synthesis in the hypothalamus
Failure of the collecting duct to respond to ADH
questions.explain: ADH levels are normal or high, but the kidney does not respond. Desmopressin does not help.

open.q: What causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

questions.q: What urine is typical of diabetes insipidus?
options: Large volumes of urine with glucose
questions.explain: The patient has polyuria and polydipsia, with low urine osmolality and no glycosuria.

open.q: What urine is typical of diabetes insipidus?

questions.q: Which diuretic impairs the countercurrent multiplier by blocking the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter?
questions.explain: Furosemide blocks the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb. This reduces medullary NaCl accumulation and weakens the osmotic gradient that normally drives water reabsorption from the collecting duct, impairing urine concentration.

open.q: Which diuretic impairs the countercurrent multiplier by blocking the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter?

questions.q: What is the lowest urine osmolality the kidney can produce (maximally dilute urine)?
questions.explain: With no ADH, the kidney can excrete urine at about 50 mOsm/L.

open.q: What is the lowest urine osmolality the kidney can produce (maximally dilute urine)?

questions.q: What is the maximum urine osmolality that a healthy human kidney can produce?
questions.explain: Humans can concentrate urine to about 1200 mOsm/kg, roughly four times plasma osmolality. Desert rodents reach much higher values because of their longer loops of Henle.

open.q: What is the maximum urine osmolality that a healthy human kidney can produce?

questions.q: What is the lowest urine osmolality the kidney can produce when ADH is completely absent?
questions.explain: Without ADH the collecting duct stays impermeable to water, so the dilute fluid from the thick ascending limb is passed on, giving urine of about 50 mOsm/kg.

open.q: What is the lowest urine osmolality the kidney can produce when ADH is completely absent?

questions.q: Which two solutes mainly create the osmotic gradient in the renal medullary interstitium?
questions.explain: NaCl accounts for most of the gradient in the outer medulla, while urea adds a large share in the inner medulla.

open.q: Which two solutes mainly create the osmotic gradient in the renal medullary interstitium?

questions.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent multiplier in the kidney?
questions.explain: The loop of Henle multiplies the small horizontal gradient created by the thick ascending limb into a large vertical gradient along the medulla. The vasa recta act as the countercurrent exchanger.

open.q: Which structure acts as the countercurrent multiplier in the kidney?
accept: Descending and ascending limbs of the nephron

questions.q: Which process in the thick ascending limb generates the single effect?
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out through the NKCC2 cotransporter but is impermeable to water. The interstitium becomes hypertonic and the tubular fluid becomes dilute.

open.q: What process in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle creates the single effect?

questions.q: At any horizontal level of the medulla, the single effect creates an osmotic difference of about:
questions.explain: The single effect is only about 200 mOsm/kg. Countercurrent flow multiplies it along the length of the loop to about 1200 mOsm/kg at the papilla.

open.q: At any horizontal level of the medulla, how large is the osmotic difference created by the single effect?
accept: About a sixth of the papillary osmolality

questions.q: The thin descending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to which substance?
questions.explain: The thin descending limb has abundant aquaporin-1 but is poorly permeable to solutes. Water leaves by osmosis and the tubular fluid becomes more concentrated as it descends.

open.q: The thin descending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to which substance?

questions.q: The thin ascending limb is permeable to NaCl but almost impermeable to which substance?
questions.explain: NaCl leaves the thin ascending limb passively down its gradient while water cannot follow. This adds solute to the medulla and dilutes the tubular fluid.

open.q: The thin ascending limb is permeable to NaCl but almost impermeable to which substance?

questions.q: Compared with plasma, what is the osmolality of the tubular fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule?
questions.explain: The fluid is diluted in the thick ascending limb to about 100 mOsm/kg whether or not ADH is present. ADH changes the osmolality only later, in the collecting duct.

open.q: Compared with plasma, what is the osmolality of the tubular fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule?

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of the osmolality of the inner medullary interstitium is due to urea?
questions.explain: Urea contributes about half of the osmolality of the inner medulla in antidiuresis. It is recycled between the collecting duct and the loop of Henle.

open.q: Approximately what fraction of the osmolality of the inner medullary interstitium is due to urea?

questions.q: Under the influence of ADH, which transporter lets urea leave the inner medullary collecting duct and enter the interstitium?
questions.explain: ADH increases the activity of UT-A1 and UT-A3 in the inner medullary collecting duct. Urea then moves into the interstitium and raises the medullary osmolality.

open.q: Under the influence of ADH, which transporter lets urea leave the inner medullary collecting duct and enter the interstitium?

questions.q: ADH increases the water permeability of the collecting duct through which second messenger?
questions.explain: ADH binds V2 receptors, which activate adenylyl cyclase through a Gs protein. The rise in cAMP triggers insertion of aquaporin-2 vesicles into the apical membrane.

open.q: ADH increases the water permeability of the collecting duct through which second messenger?

questions.q: Water entering collecting duct principal cells through aquaporin-2 leaves across the basolateral membrane through which channel?
questions.explain: AQP3 and AQP4 are constitutively present in the basolateral membrane. AQP2 is the ADH-regulated channel in the apical membrane.

open.q: Water entering collecting duct principal cells through aquaporin-2 leaves across the basolateral membrane through which channels?

questions.q: Which vessels preserve the medullary osmotic gradient by acting as countercurrent exchangers?
questions.explain: The vasa recta are hairpin capillaries that run alongside the loops of Henle. Solutes and water exchange between their two limbs, so little solute is carried out of the medulla.

open.q: Which vessels preserve the medullary osmotic gradient by acting as countercurrent exchangers?
accept: Vessels running alongside the loops of Henle

questions.q: Why is blood flow in the vasa recta kept low?
options: To reduce oxygen delivery to the cortex
To limit solute washout from the medulla
To increase the glomerular filtration rate
To block urea reaching the interstitium
questions.explain: Medullary blood flow is only 1 to 2% of renal blood flow. A high flow would wash solutes out of the medulla and flatten the gradient, but the low flow makes the medulla prone to hypoxia.

open.q: Why is blood flow in the vasa recta kept low?
accept: To prevent washout of the medullary gradient

questions.q: Furosemide reduces the ability to concentrate urine mainly because it:
options: Blocks water channels in the duct
Increases ADH breakdown in the liver
Raises urea delivery to the loop
questions.explain: Furosemide blocks NKCC2, so the single effect is lost and the medullary gradient falls. The urine becomes close to isotonic.

open.q: By what mechanism does furosemide reduce the ability to concentrate urine?
accept: Washout of the medullary osmotic gradient
Blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb

questions.q: A healthy man excretes 600 mOsm of solute daily, and his maximum urine osmolality is 1200 mOsm/kg. What is the minimum urine volume he must pass per day?
questions.explain: The minimum (obligatory) urine volume equals the solute load divided by the maximum urine osmolality: 600 divided by 1200 gives 0.5 L.

open.q: A healthy man excretes 600 mOsm of solute daily, and his maximum urine osmolality is 1200 mOsm/kg. What is the minimum urine volume he must pass per day?

questions.q: During maximal antidiuresis, free water clearance is:
questions.explain: Free water clearance is urine flow minus osmolar clearance. In antidiuresis the urine is hypertonic, so osmolar clearance exceeds urine flow and the value is below zero.

open.q: During maximal antidiuresis, what is the sign of free water clearance?

questions.q: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus passes large volumes of urine. Which mechanism is responsible for the polyuria?
questions.explain: Glucose that exceeds the transport maximum stays in the tubule and holds water in the lumen. The result is a solute diuresis with raised urine osmolality, unlike diabetes insipidus.

open.q: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus passes large volumes of urine. Which mechanism is responsible for the polyuria?
accept: Unreabsorbed glucose holding water in the tubule
Osmotic effect of glucose in the tubule

questions.q: A patient with polyuria and polydipsia is water-deprived and urine osmolality stays at 150 mOsm/kg. After desmopressin it rises to 600 mOsm/kg. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: A good response to desmopressin shows the kidney can respond to ADH but the pituitary is not making it. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus would show no response.

open.q: A patient with polyuria and polydipsia is water-deprived and urine osmolality stays at 150 mOsm/kg. After desmopressin it rises to 600 mOsm/kg. What is the diagnosis?

questions.q: A patient on long-term lithium has dilute urine that does not concentrate after desmopressin. Which defect is most likely?
options: Absent secretion of ADH from the pituitary
Loss of blood flow in the vasa recta
Excess sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule
questions.explain: Lithium impairs the response of the principal cells to ADH and reduces aquaporin-2 expression, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

open.q: A patient on long-term lithium has dilute urine that does not concentrate after desmopressin. Which defect is most likely?

questions.q: A woman drinks 12 litres of water daily and has low serum sodium and very dilute urine. After water deprivation her urine concentrates normally. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: Excess water intake suppresses ADH appropriately, so the urine is dilute. When water is restricted, ADH rises and the kidneys concentrate normally.

open.q: A woman drinks 12 litres of water daily and has low serum sodium and very dilute urine. After water deprivation her urine concentrates normally. What is the diagnosis?

questions.q: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease has urine osmolality fixed near 300 mOsm/kg whatever the hydration. What is this called?
questions.explain: Isosthenuria means urine of fixed osmolality equal to plasma. Damaged nephrons lose the countercurrent mechanism, so the kidney can neither concentrate nor dilute.

open.q: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease has urine osmolality fixed near 300 mOsm/kg whatever the hydration. What is this called?
accept: Loss of concentrating and diluting ability

questions.q: Prolonged high urine flow reduces maximal concentrating ability mainly because of:
questions.explain: A high flow through the medulla washes out urea and NaCl from the interstitium. The gradient takes hours to days to rebuild.

open.q: Prolonged high urine flow reduces maximal concentrating ability mainly because of which process?
accept: Dissipation of the medullary osmotic gradient

questions.q: Which water channel is constitutively present in the proximal tubule and the thin descending limb?
questions.explain: Aquaporin-1 is not regulated by ADH and gives these segments high water permeability. Aquaporin-2 is the ADH-regulated channel of the collecting duct.

open.q: Which water channel is constitutively present in the proximal tubule and the thin descending limb?

questions.q: Which nephron segment becomes water permeable under the influence of ADH?
questions.explain: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane of principal cells in the late distal tubule and collecting duct. The thick ascending limb stays water-impermeable.

open.q: Which nephron segment becomes water permeable under the influence of ADH?
accept: Principal cells of the collecting duct
Late distal tubule and collecting duct

questions.q: A malnourished patient on a very low-protein diet cannot concentrate urine well, although ADH is normal. Which mechanism is mainly impaired?
options: Active NaCl transport in the thick ascending limb
Urea recycling to the medullary interstitium
questions.explain: Low protein intake reduces urea production, so less urea is available to build the inner medullary gradient. Concentrating ability returns when protein intake is restored.

open.q: A malnourished patient on a very low-protein diet cannot concentrate urine well, although ADH is normal. Which mechanism is mainly impaired?
accept: Low urea in the inner medulla

questions.q: Why does the osmolality of tubular fluid rise as it descends the thin descending limb?
options: Potassium is secreted into the lumen
NaCl is secreted into the lumen
Glucose is added to the lumen
questions.explain: The interstitium becomes progressively more hypertonic with depth, so water moves out through aquaporin-1. The remaining fluid becomes more concentrated.

open.q: Why does the osmolality of tubular fluid rise as it descends the thin descending limb?
accept: Water loss to the hypertonic interstitium

questions.q: At which point is the tubular fluid osmolality highest during antidiuresis?
options: Start of the thick ascending limb
Midpoint of the thick ascending limb
Tip of the loop in the papilla
questions.explain: Fluid in the loop equilibrates with the interstitium, so it reaches its highest osmolality, about 1200 mOsm/kg, at the hairpin bend deep in the medulla.

open.q: At which point along the loop of Henle is the tubular fluid osmolality highest during antidiuresis?
accept: Bottom of the loop of Henle

questions.q: Alcohol increases urine volume mainly because it:
options: Blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
Inhibits ADH release from the pituitary
questions.explain: Alcohol suppresses ADH secretion, so the collecting duct stays water-impermeable and a water diuresis follows. This is why dilute urine is passed after drinking.

open.q: By what mechanism does alcohol increase urine volume?

questions.q: A patient with prolonged poor protein intake has a reduced ability to produce concentrated urine despite an adequate rise in ADH. Which medullary solute contribution is most likely reduced?
questions.explain: Urea recycling contributes substantially to inner medullary interstitial hyperosmolality. Low protein intake reduces urea generation and can impair maximal urine-concentrating ability even when ADH secretion is intact.

questions.q: Why does the descending limb of the vasa recta gain solute and lose water as it travels into the renal medulla?
options: It passively equilibrates with the progressively hyperosmotic medullary interstitium
ADH actively pumps sodium into the vessel
The vasa recta actively secretes urea into the tubular lumen
Glomerular filtration continues along the vessel
questions.explain: The vasa recta are countercurrent exchangers. As blood descends into the hyperosmotic medulla, water diffuses out and solutes diffuse in; the reverse occurs during ascent, limiting washout of the gradient.

questions.q: A patient with central diabetes insipidus receives desmopressin. Which change is expected in the collecting ducts?
options: Insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane
Removal of aquaporin-2 channels from the apical membrane
Reduced water permeability despite increased cAMP
questions.explain: Desmopressin activates V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells, increasing cAMP and promoting insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane, thereby increasing water reabsorption.

questions.q: Which nephron segment remains essentially impermeable to water even when circulating ADH is high, while continuing to reabsorb NaCl?
options: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs NaCl through NKCC2 but is effectively water-impermeable. This dilutes tubular fluid and helps establish the medullary osmotic gradient.

questions.q: A patient with severe hypercalcaemia develops polyuria and cannot concentrate urine appropriately. Which mechanism best explains this effect?
options: Impaired renal response to ADH, producing a nephrogenic diabetes-insipidus-like state
Excessive insertion of aquaporin-2 in collecting ducts
Increased urea recycling in the inner medulla
Increased water permeability of the thick ascending limb
questions.explain: Hypercalcaemia can impair collecting-duct responsiveness to ADH and reduce aquaporin-2 expression or function, causing a nephrogenic diabetes-insipidus-like concentrating defect.
